title: Concepts & Revision Bank
description: Core JS / React / HTML / CSS / Analytics concept recall for quick revision.

questions.question: Which engine powers BOTH Google Chrome and Node.js?
questions.explanation: V8 is Google's open-source engine used inside Chrome and as the core of Node.js.

questions.question: What is the first stage a JS engine performs after reading source code?

options.text: Execute it line by line immediately
Parse it into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)

questions.explanation: The Parser tokenizes and validates syntax, producing an AST before compilation/execution.

questions.question: JIT stands for Just-In-Time. What does JIT compilation do in V8?

options.text: Interprets code once and discards it

questions.explanation: V8 uses Ignition (interpreter) + Turbofan (optimizing compiler) to optimize hot code at runtime.

questions.question: Is Node.js a JavaScript engine?

options.text: No, Node.js is a runtime that embeds the V8 engine

questions.explanation: Node.js is a runtime (V8 + libuv + C++ addons). The engine inside it is V8.

questions.question: Which component of the engine reclaims unused memory automatically?
questions.explanation: V8's garbage collector (minor/major) reclaims unreachable objects from the heap.

questions.question: What commonly causes V8 to DEOPTIMIZE (revert optimized code to slower code)?

options.text: Reassigning a variable to a different type in a hot path

questions.explanation: Type changes break inline caches / hidden classes, forcing deoptimization of hot functions.

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE about the Event Loop?

options.text: It is part of the JavaScript language spec
It is provided by the runtime environment (browser/Node), not the engine itself

questions.explanation: The Event Loop is runtime-provided (libuv in Node, browser APIs). The engine handles execution contexts & call stack.

questions.question: In Angular, what does Zone.js patching help the engine/runtime trigger?
questions.explanation: Zone.js monkey-patches async APIs so Angular knows when to run change detection.

questions.question: A Promise that has settled successfully is in which state?
questions.explanation: Once resolved with a value, a Promise is 'fulfilled' (resolved and successful).

questions.question: What does .then() return?
questions.explanation: then/catch/finally return new Promises, which is what makes promise chaining possible.

questions.question: What is returned by Promise.all if ANY input promise rejects?

options.text: An array with nulls for the rejected ones
It rejects immediately with that rejection reason
It waits for all then resolves

questions.explanation: Promise.all is fail-fast: one rejection rejects the whole combined promise.

questions.question: Which static method resolves as soon as the FIRST promise settles (fulfilled OR rejected)?
questions.explanation: Promise.race settles on the first settled promise regardless of fulfill/reject.

questions.question: What does Promise.allSettled resolve with?

options.text: An array of result objects {status:'fulfilled'|'rejected', value|reason}

questions.explanation: allSettled waits for ALL promises and reports each outcome, never short-circuiting.

questions.question: A Promise executor function receives two arguments. What are they?
questions.explanation: new Promise((resolve, reject) => {...}) — call resolve(value) or reject(reason).

questions.question: What will `Promise.resolve(5).then(x => { throw x })` produce?
questions.explanation: Throwing inside a then callback rejects the returned promise (caught by a following .catch).

questions.question: Callbacks passed to then/catch always run as...?
questions.explanation: Promise reactions are microtasks, queued in the microtask queue and drained before rendering/macrotasks.

questions.question: What does an `async function` ALWAYS return?

options.text: A Promise that resolves to the returned value

questions.explanation: async functions wrap the return value in a Promise automatically.

questions.question: If you `await` a rejected promise, what happens?

options.text: It throws inside the async function (catchable with try/catch)

questions.explanation: An awaited rejection throws at the await point; wrap in try/catch to handle it.

questions.question: To run two independent async calls in PARALLEL with async/await, you should...
questions.explanation: Start both promises, then await Promise.all so they run concurrently, not sequentially.

questions.question: `await` can only be used inside...?

options.text: An async function (or top-level await in modules)

questions.explanation: await is only valid inside async functions (or module top-level await).

questions.question: Under the hood, async/await is built on top of...?
questions.explanation: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promise chaining, making async code read like sync code.

questions.question: What does `await` actually do to the surrounding code?

options.text: Blocks the main thread until done
Suspends the async function, yielding control back to the event loop

questions.explanation: await pauses the async function (non-blocking); other code keeps running via the event loop.

questions.question: If a function is marked `async` but never uses `await`, it still...
questions.explanation: The async keyword alone forces Promise-return semantics regardless of await usage.

questions.question: Which is the BEST pattern for handling multiple awaits that may each fail independently?

options.text: try/catch per step OR Promise.allSettled then inspect each result

questions.explanation: Per-step try/catch or allSettled gives granular control over which operations succeeded.

questions.question: What is the correct ordering of the queues in the event loop?

options.text: Microtasks (drain fully) run before the next macrotask

questions.explanation: After the current task, the microtask queue is fully drained before the next macrotask and before rendering.

questions.question: Which of these is a MACROtask (not a microtask)?
questions.explanation: setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate are macrotasks; promise reactions, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver are microtasks.
Sync logs 1 and 4; promise microtask (3) runs before the setTimeout macrotask (2).

questions.question: Who provides the Event Loop — the JS engine (V8) or the runtime (browser/Node)?
questions.explanation: The Event Loop is part of the host runtime (libuv in Node, browser), not the ECMAScript spec/engine.

questions.question: What is the danger of an infinite chain of microtasks?

options.text: It starves the macrotask queue and UI rendering (page freezes)

questions.explanation: Because microtasks drain fully before macrotasks/rendering, an infinite microtask loop blocks the UI.

questions.question: In Node.js, which is generally processed before timers (setTimeout)?
questions.explanation: Node runs the microtask queue between each phase of its loop, so pending promise reactions run before timers.

questions.question: What do arrow functions NOT have of their own?

options.text: Their own 'this' binding (they inherit lexical this)

questions.explanation: Arrow functions capture 'this' from the enclosing scope — no own this, arguments, super, or new.target.

questions.question: Can you use `new` with an arrow function?

options.text: No — arrow functions are not constructors
Only if it has a body

questions.explanation: Arrows lack [[Construct]], so calling them with new throws a TypeError.

questions.question: Which arrow syntax implicitly returns a value (no 'return' keyword)?
questions.explanation: A concise-body arrow (no braces) implicitly returns its single expression.

questions.question: Inside an arrow function, what is `arguments`?

options.text: The arguments of the enclosing (lexical) function, or undefined in module scope

questions.explanation: Arrows have no own 'arguments'; they reference the outer function's arguments object.

questions.question: Why are arrow functions a poor choice for object methods that need `this`?

options.text: They do not bind 'this' to the object, so 'this' is the enclosing scope

questions.explanation: object.method = () => this.x uses lexical this (outer scope), not the method's receiver — typically unwanted.

questions.question: How do you return an object literal concisely with an arrow function?
questions.explanation: Wrap the literal in parentheses so {} is parsed as an object, not a block body.

questions.question: const { a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 }; — what is `b`?
questions.explanation: Object destructuring binds variables to same-named properties.

questions.question: How do you rename while destructuring? e.g. bind `name` to property `user`?
questions.explanation: The syntax { sourceProperty: targetVariable } renames during destructuring.

questions.question: const [x, , y] = [1, 2, 3]; — what is `y`?
questions.explanation: The empty slot skips index 1; y binds to index 2 (value 3).

questions.question: const { a = 10 } = {}; — what is `a`?
questions.explanation: Default values apply when the property is undefined (here {} has no 'a').

questions.question: const { a: { b } } = { a: { b: 5 } }; — what is `b`?
questions.explanation: Nested destructuring reaches into the nested object to bind inner property b.

questions.question: Which is a valid use of destructuring in a function parameter?
questions.explanation: You can destructure the incoming object directly in the parameter list — common for options objects.

questions.question: What is the key difference between an `interface` and a `type` alias in TypeScript?

options.text: They are completely identical with no differences
Interfaces are extendable/merged via declaration merging; type aliases cannot be reopened
type aliases can only hold primitives
Interfaces compile to JavaScript; type aliases do not

questions.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging and 'extends'; type aliases are closed and support unions/intersections better.

questions.question: Which is a valid way to make a property optional in an interface?
questions.explanation: The ? postfix marks an optional property.

questions.question: Can an interface describe a function signature?
questions.explanation: Interfaces can declare call signatures, index signatures, and construct signatures.

questions.question: Declaration merging means...

options.text: Two interface declarations with the same name are combined
Interfaces are minified at build time
They are deleted from the output

questions.explanation: Multiple interface declarations with the same name merge — useful for ambient/global augmentation.

questions.question: An interface with only an index signature `interface Dict { [k: string]: number }` means...?

options.text: Any string key maps to a number value

questions.explanation: Index signatures describe the type of all properties accessed by that key type.

questions.question: Which is preferred for describing React/Angular component props in most codebases?

options.text: An interface (e.g. Props) or type alias — both common

questions.explanation: Both interface and type alias work for props; convention varies by team.

questions.question: What must be enabled to use decorators in TypeScript (pre-5.x)?

options.text: Nothing, they are on by default

questions.explanation: Decorators are experimental; set experimentalDecorators:true (and often emitDecoratorMetadata) to use them.

questions.question: A class decorator receives what as its argument?
questions.explanation: Class decorators receive the constructor function and can return a new constructor to replace it.

questions.question: Which decorator is used by Angular on components?
questions.explanation: Angular's @Component() decorator attaches metadata (template, selector, styles) to the class.

questions.question: A method decorator's signature is (target, propertyKey, descriptor). What is `descriptor`?

options.text: The PropertyDescriptor of the method (can wrap value)

questions.explanation: The descriptor lets you replace/ wrap the method via descriptor.value (e.g. for logging or memoization).

questions.question: Decorators in TC39 proposals apply in which order for nested cases?

options.text: Bottom-up / inside-out for evaluation, but declaration order for lists

questions.explanation: Evaluation is inside-out (inner decorators run first), but the decorator EXPRESSIONS are evaluated outside-in.

questions.question: Why does Angular need emitDecoratorMetadata?

options.text: To emit design:type metadata so DI can infer constructor param types

questions.explanation: Angular's DI uses emitted metadata (design:paramtypes) to resolve dependencies by type at runtime.

questions.question: Which of these is a SEMANTIC element (conveys meaning), not just a generic container?
questions.explanation:
describes self-contained content.
/ are generic and carry no meaning;
is a line break.

questions.question: How many <main> elements should a single HTML document contain?

options.text: None is required, but max three

questions.explanation: There must be exactly ONE <main> per document — it represents the dominant unique content. Multiple <main> elements break assistive-tech expectations.

questions.question: What implicit ARIA role does the <nav> element expose to assistive technology?
questions.explanation: Browsers map <nav> to role="navigation". <header>→banner, <footer>→contentinfo, <section>→region.

questions.question: Which element should wrap an independent, reusable piece of content (e.g. a blog post or comment)?
questions.explanation: <article> marks content that is independently distributable (posts, comments, cards). <section> groups thematically related content; <aside> is tangential.

questions.question: Why does semantic HTML help SEO?

options.text: It makes the page load faster
Search crawlers infer structure/meaning and rank content better
It removes the need for meta tags

questions.explanation: Crawlers use semantics to understand hierarchy and topic relevance, improving indexing/ranking. It is not a direct speed or font effect.

questions.question: A common mistake is using <section> purely for styling. What is the correct rule?

options.text: Use <section> only when it has a heading and groups related content
Use <section> for every box you want to style
Nest as many <main> as needed inside <section>

questions.explanation: A section should group thematically related content, typically with a heading. For pure styling use <div>. Never nest multiple <main>.

questions.question: What does the <time> element with a datetime attribute provide?

options.text: A live clock on the page
Machine-readable date/time for parsers and search engines

questions.explanation: <time datetime="..."> gives parsers/search engines a standardized value (e.g. 2025-01-01T09:00Z) while showing human text inside.

questions.question: In Angular templates, why is using semantic tags (article/header/footer) recommended?

options.text: It produces accessible, well-structured component layouts
It is required by Angular CLI
It removes the need for RxJS

questions.explanation: Semantic tags in component templates give accessible, maintainable structure — a frontend best practice, not an Angular requirement.

questions.question: What does a11y stand for and what problem does it solve?

options.text: Accessibility; making digital experiences usable by people with disabilities

questions.explanation: a11y = accessibility (a + 11 letters + y). It ensures people with visual/auditory/motor/cognitive impairments can use the product.

questions.question: Which is the BEST practice when building a custom clickable component?

options.text: Use <div role="button" tabindex="0"> and re-implement keyboard handling
Use <span onclick> with no keyboard support

questions.explanation: Native <button> gives focus, keyboard (Enter/Space), and role for free. ARIA should only be added when native elements can't be used (first rule of ARIA).

questions.question: An image used purely for decoration should be made invisible to screen readers by:
questions.explanation: Empty alt="" tells assistive tech to ignore the image. Descriptive alt is for meaningful images; missing alt is an a11y failure.

questions.question: What does the 'first rule of ARIA' state?

options.text: Always use role attributes on every element
Use native HTML elements with built-in semantics before reaching for ARIA
ARIA overrides everything, so use it liberally

questions.explanation: First rule: if a native element or attribute has the semantics you need, use it instead of ARIA, which can override and break native behavior.

questions.question: Which Angular CDK utility announces dynamic changes to screen-reader users?
questions.explanation: LiveAnnouncer (from @angular/cdk/a11y) pushes text to an aria-live region so SR users hear updates like 'Item added to cart'.

questions.question: A modal dialog must trap focus. Why?

options.text: To prevent the user from scrolling the background
So keyboard users cannot escape into background content while the dialog is open

questions.explanation: Focus trapping keeps keyboard/Tab navigation inside the modal so users don't lose context in background content — a core a11y requirement.

questions.question: Which is a common accessibility mistake?

options.text: Missing alt text on informative images

questions.explanation: Missing alt text, poor contrast, and non-keyboard-operable controls are the classic a11y failures to avoid.

questions.question: What do browser accessibility APIs (AXAPI/UIA/AT-SPI) do?

options.text: Expose accessible names/states from the DOM to assistive technologies

questions.explanation: The accessibility tree (built from DOM + ARIA) is exposed via platform APIs so screen readers can announce names, roles, and states.

questions.question: What does ARIA stand for and what does it provide?

options.text: Accessible Rich Internet Applications; roles/states/properties for accessibility

questions.explanation: ARIA = Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It adds role, aria-* state, and property attributes for widgets native HTML can't express.

questions.question: Which attribute would you use to tell a screen reader the CURRENT value of a custom slider (min 0, max 100, now 50)?
questions.explanation: For role="slider" you expose aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax so SRs announce the live value range.

questions.question: What does aria-live="polite" do?

options.text: Announces dynamic content changes to SR users without interrupting current speech

questions.explanation: aria-live regions announce updates. 'polite' queues after current speech; 'assertive' interrupts. Essential for toasts/status updates.

questions.question: A key pitfall: <div role="button"> is NOT clickable by itself. Why?

options.text: Because role adds full functionality automatically
Because role only changes the accessibility tree; you must add JS for click + keyboard (Enter/Space)
Because it requires a form wrapper

questions.explanation: ARIA role is semantic only — it does not add behavior. A <button> gives click + Enter/Space for free; a div needs manual JS.

questions.question: When should you AVOID using ARIA?

options.text: On every element to be safe
When a native HTML element already provides the needed semantics
Never; ARIA is always better than HTML

questions.explanation: First rule of ARIA: prefer native HTML. Adding ARIA can override and break native semantics if done incorrectly.

questions.question: In a tab interface, which ARIA pattern is correct for the selected tab?
questions.explanation: Tabs use role="tab" with aria-selected (true/false) and aria-controls pointing to the associated tabpanel — follows WAI-ARIA APG.

questions.question: What is aria-hidden="true" used for?

options.text: To hide content visually from all users
To remove an element from the accessibility tree (SR ignores it) while still showing it visually
To delete the element from DOM

questions.explanation: aria-hidden removes a node from the a11y tree (e.g. decorative icons) but keeps it visible. Never put aria-hidden on focusable content.

questions.question: Which Angular library relies heavily on ARIA patterns for keyboard nav & screen readers?
questions.explanation: Angular Material components (Menu, Dialog, Tabs, CDK Overlay) implement WAI-ARIA patterns for accessibility out of the box.

questions.question: SEO stands for:
questions.explanation: SEO improves a site's visibility in organic (non-paid) search results via content, technical, and authority signals.

questions.question: The three core stages a search engine follows are:
questions.explanation: Bots crawl URLs, index parsed content, then rank pages by relevance/authority for a query.

questions.question: A <link rel='canonical'> tells search engines:

options.text: Which URL is the preferred/authoritative version of duplicate content

questions.explanation: Canonical URLs consolidate ranking signals and avoid duplicate-content penalties across near-identical pages.

questions.question: Structured data (schema.org JSON-LD) is used to:

options.text: Help search engines understand content and enable rich results (snippets)

questions.explanation: Schema markup lets Google show rich results (ratings, FAQs). JSON-LD is the recommended format.

questions.question: For SPAs (like Angular), the main SEO challenge is:

options.text: Content is rendered client-side, so crawlers may not see it without SSR/prerendering

questions.explanation: Client-rendered HTML can be empty when crawled; SSR (Angular Universal) or prerendering fixes crawlability.

questions.question: Keyword stuffing is harmful because it:

options.text: Reads unnaturally and can trigger search-engine spam penalties

questions.explanation: Overusing keywords looks spammy; modern algorithms reward natural, relevant content over density.

questions.question: Core Web Vitals influence SEO because they measure:
questions.explanation: LCP, FID/INP, and CLS are page-experience signals that Google factors into rankings.

questions.question: Mobile-first indexing means Google primarily:

options.text: Uses the mobile version of a page for ranking and indexing

questions.explanation: Since most searches are mobile, Google indexes the mobile rendering first — responsive, mobile-friendly pages matter.

questions.question: The <label for='email'> associates with an input via the input's:
questions.explanation: for must equal the target input's id. Proper labels improve a11y and clickable area.

questions.question: To send form data via the URL (GET) vs body (POST), you use:
questions.explanation: method controls how data is submitted; GET appends to URL (idempotent, bookmarkable), POST sends in body (for mutations).

questions.question: The 'name' attribute on an input is important because it:

options.text: Identifies the field's key in submitted form data

questions.explanation: Only inputs with a name are submitted; name becomes the key (e.g. email=value) in the payload.

questions.question: required on an input:

options.text: Blocks native form submission until the field is filled

questions.explanation: The required attribute triggers built-in browser validation before submit — no JS needed for the basic check.

questions.question: The 'placeholder' attribute shows:

options.text: Hint text inside the field that disappears on input (not a label substitute)

questions.explanation: Placeholder is a hint only; always provide a real <label> for accessibility — placeholders vanish and aren't announced as labels.

questions.question: A fieldset/legend is useful for:

options.text: Grouping related controls with an accessible group label

questions.explanation: fieldset + legend semantically groups radios/checkboxes and is announced by screen readers as a group.

questions.question: For accessibility, each input should have:
questions.explanation: A real label (or aria-label) lets screen readers announce the field's purpose; placeholder/title alone is insufficient.

questions.question: novalidate on a <form> does:

options.text: Disables native browser validation (lets you handle it in JS)

questions.explanation: novalidate skips built-in checks — useful when you run custom Angular/JS validation and don't want double prompts.

questions.question: Why prefer type="email" over type="text" for an email field?

options.text: It gives native validation (@ check), email keyboard on mobile, and autofill hints
It prevents all invalid input permanently

questions.explanation: Semantic input types trigger browser validation, optimized mobile keyboards, and password-manager/autofill detection.

questions.question: Which attribute restricts a number input to values between 1 and 10?
questions.explanation: min/max set the allowed bounds for number/range/date inputs. step controls increment granularity.

questions.question: What does input type="range" render and what attributes control it?

options.text: A text box; controlled by size
A slider; min, max, step, value

questions.explanation: type="range" shows a slider bounded by min/max with step increments; value sets the initial position.

questions.question: A file input with accept=".pdf,.docx" multiple allows users to:

options.text: Select multiple files filtered to PDF/DOCX types

questions.explanation: accept hints the file picker filter; multiple enables selecting several files. The actual upload needs a form/JS.

questions.question: If a browser doesn't support type="date", what happens?

options.text: It falls back to a plain text input

questions.explanation: Unknown input types degrade gracefully to type="text", so you should still validate server-side and/or with JS.

questions.question: Which input type triggers a numeric keypad with symbols (good for phone numbers)?
questions.explanation: type="tel" shows a telephone-optimized numeric keypad. type="number" can also show digits but tel is semantically for phone.

questions.question: What is the <input type="color"> element used for?

options.text: Opening a native color picker returning a hex value like #ff0000

questions.explanation: type="color" opens a color picker and the value is a hex string (e.g. #ff0000).

questions.question: Even with built-in validation, why must you STILL validate on the server?

options.text: Because client-side validation can be bypassed (disabled JS, crafted requests)

questions.explanation: Client validation is a UX convenience and is trivially bypassed; authoritative validation must happen server-side.

questions.question: The <canvas> element is a:

options.text: Scriptable bitmap drawing surface (pixels drawn via JS)

questions.explanation: Canvas is a blank bitmap you paint on imperatively with the 2D (or WebGL) context — pixel-based, not DOM-based.

questions.question: To draw on canvas you first get:
questions.explanation: getContext('2d') returns the drawing API (fillRect, moveTo, etc.). For 3D you'd request 'webgl'.

questions.question: ctx.fillRect(10, 20, 100, 50) draws a rectangle at:
questions.explanation: fillRect(x, y, w, h): top-left corner at (x,y), then width/height. Origin is top-left, y grows downward.

questions.question: Canvas differs from SVG in that it is:

options.text: Immediate-mode raster (no retained object model; redraw to change)

questions.explanation: SVG keeps addressable DOM nodes; canvas paints pixels and forgets them — you must redraw to animate/update.

questions.question: On high-DPI (Retina) screens, the common fix is:

options.text: Scale canvas.width/height by devicePixelRatio and ctx.scale(ratio, ratio)

questions.explanation: Without ratio scaling, canvas bitmaps look blurry on retina. Multiply backing store by DPR, scale the context, keep CSS size constant.

questions.question: When animating, you should clear the previous frame with:
questions.explanation: clearRect wipes the bitmap each frame so old drawings don't smear; then redraw the new state.

questions.question: ctx.beginPath(), moveTo(), lineTo(), stroke() draws:
questions.explanation: beginPath starts a new path; moveTo/lineTo define points; stroke() renders the outline (fill() would paint it).

questions.question: Chart.js and similar libraries render via:
questions.explanation: Most 2D charting libs paint to canvas for performance with many data points; some offer an SVG renderer too.

questions.question: SVG stands for:
questions.explanation: SVG is an XML-based vector format that scales without quality loss — resolution independent.

questions.question: A key advantage over <canvas> is SVG is:

options.text: Retained-mode (DOM nodes) — each shape is selectable, styleable, and accessible

questions.explanation: SVG elements are real DOM nodes (can be targeted by CSS/JS, given ARIA). Canvas is an opaque bitmap.

questions.question: An SVG drawn with <circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40'> places its center at:
questions.explanation: cx/cy are the center coordinates; r is the radius. SVG origin is top-left, y downward like canvas.

questions.question: SVG scales crisply because it is:

options.text: Vector math (paths/curves), not a fixed pixel grid

questions.explanation: Vectors are recalculated at any size, so no pixelation — ideal for logos and icons.

questions.question: You can style SVG via:

options.text: CSS (fill, stroke) and/or presentation attributes (fill=, stroke=)

questions.explanation: Both CSS properties and SVG attributes control fill/stroke; CSS classes let you theme icons easily.

questions.question: SVG vs an icon: inline SVG lets you:

options.text: Recolor/animate/manipulate it with CSS and JS at runtime

questions.explanation: Inlining SVG makes each path a DOM node — you can change fill on hover, animate paths, add a11y. is opaque.

questions.question: For accessibility, an inline SVG icon should usually have:
questions.explanation: Meaningful icons need an accessible name; purely decorative ones should be aria-hidden to avoid noise.

questions.question: A common use case best suited to SVG is:

options.text: Logos, icons, and diagrams that must stay sharp at any size

questions.explanation: SVG excels at sharp, small, animatable vector art; use canvas/raster for photos and heavy pixel work.

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of Shadow DOM?

options.text: To provide style and markup encapsulation (scoping) for a component
To store component state in a database

questions.explanation: Shadow DOM creates a scoped subtree so internal styles/markup don't leak out and page styles don't bleed in — the basis of Web Components.

questions.question: What is the 'shadow host'?

options.text: The regular DOM element that a shadow root is attached to

questions.explanation: The shadow host is the ordinary element (e.g. <my-element>) to which a shadow root is attached, becoming the container for the shadow tree.

questions.question: Which CSS selector targets the shadow HOST from inside the shadow tree?
questions.explanation: :host selects the host element from within the shadow DOM. ::slotted() targets light-DOM children projected via <slot>.

questions.question: How are child elements passed from the light DOM into a shadow tree?
questions.explanation: <slot> elements in the shadow tree define where and how light-DOM children are distributed (composed) into the shadow content.

questions.question: What is 'event retargeting' in Shadow DOM?

options.text: Events crossing the shadow boundary are reported with the nearest non-shadow ancestor as target

questions.explanation: To preserve encapsulation, when an event crosses out of a shadow tree, its target is retargeted to the shadow host rather than internal nodes.

questions.question: In Angular, View Encapsulation uses Shadow DOM style scoping. Which mode uses the real Shadow DOM?
questions.explanation: ViewEncapsulation.ShadowDom attaches a real shadow root. The default Emulated fakes scoping with attribute selectors for broader support.

questions.question: Why might you choose 'open' shadow mode over 'closed'?

options.text: Open exposes shadowRoot for testing/tooling; closed hides it and breaks testability

questions.explanation: Open mode lets element.shadowRoot be accessed (tests, devtools, libraries). Closed mode hides it, hurting testability with little real security gain.

questions.question: Do CSS selectors from the main document reach INSIDE a shadow root?

options.text: No — styles inside don't leak out and outside selectors can't reach in (unless ::part/::slotted)

questions.explanation: Shadow DOM enforces style scoping: internal styles stay in, external selectors stay out. ::part() and ::slotted() are the sanctioned bridges.

questions.question: Which is the strongest approach for accessibility?

options.text: Start with semantic native HTML, add ARIA only where needed
Rely on color alone to convey meaning
Skip keyboard support for mouse-only users

questions.explanation: Native semantics first, ARIA as a supplement. ARIA used incorrectly can harm more than help (first rule of ARIA).

questions.question: WCAG's four principles are often remembered as POUR. What does POUR stand for?
questions.explanation: POUR = Perceivable (info present), Operable (keyboard/navigable), Understandable (clear), Robust (works with AT).

questions.question: Keyboard accessibility requires that:

options.text: All functionality is reachable and operable via keyboard

questions.explanation: Every interactive element must be focusable and operable with keyboard (Enter/Space/arrows), with a visible focus indicator.

questions.question: For a complex widget (e.g. combobox), you should:

options.text: Build it with divs and skip roles
Follow the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices pattern (roles, states, keyboard)
Disable screen readers on that component

questions.explanation: Complex widgets need the documented APG pattern: correct roles, aria states, and full keyboard interaction.

questions.question: What is a 'focus indicator' and why does it matter?

options.text: The visible outline showing which element is focused — essential for keyboard users

questions.explanation: Removing default focus outlines without a replacement breaks keyboard navigation. Never do outline:none without an alternative.

questions.question: How should dynamic content (e.g. '3 items added') be announced to SR users?

options.text: Push it into an aria-live region (polite/assertive)
Append to the title tag only

questions.explanation: aria-live regions announce changes. LiveAnnouncer in Angular CDK is a common implementation.

questions.question: Color contrast minimum (WCAG AA, normal text) is roughly:
questions.explanation: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 contrast for normal text, 3:1 for large text. Poor contrast is a top a11y failure.

questions.question: Which tool is commonly used to AUDIT accessibility?
questions.explanation: Automated tools (axe, WAVE, Lighthouse) catch many issues; combine with manual testing using NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver.

questions.question: Why have traditional SPAs struggled with SEO?

options.text: Because content is rendered client-side via JS, which crawlers may not execute in time

questions.explanation: Crawlers that don't fully execute JS (or time out) see an empty shell, so JS-rendered content may not be indexed.

questions.question: SSR (Server-Side Rendering) helps SPA SEO by:

options.text: Sending pre-rendered HTML so crawlers see content immediately

questions.explanation: SSR (e.g. Angular Universal) returns full HTML from the server, making content visible to crawlers and improving first paint.

questions.question: What is the tradeoff between SSG and SSR?

options.text: SSG builds static HTML at build time (fast, great for fixed content); SSR renders per-request (fresh, dynamic)
SSG requires a database per request

questions.explanation: SSG pre-renders at build time (ideal for blogs/docs); SSR renders on each request (ideal for personalized/dynamic pages).

questions.question: Why is structured data (schema.org JSON-LD) valuable for SEO?

options.text: It lets search engines show rich results (ratings, breadcrumbs, FAQs)

questions.explanation: JSON-LD structured data helps Google produce rich snippets (Article, Product, FAQ), improving visibility/CTR.

questions.question: How do you set per-route <title> and meta tags in an Angular SPA?

options.text: Using the Title and Meta services, often with a route resolver/guard
They cannot be changed per route

questions.explanation: Angular's Title/Meta services update document head dynamically per route; with SSR this is also sent server-side.

questions.question: A canonical URL (rel="canonical") is used to:

options.text: Tell search engines which version of a URL is the authoritative one (avoid duplicate content)

questions.explanation: Canonical tags consolidate duplicate/similar URLs so ranking signals point to one preferred page.

questions.question: Social media preview cards (Open Graph) require:

options.text: OG meta tags in the served HTML head (needs SSR/prerender for SPAs)

questions.explanation: og:title/og:image etc. must be present in the HTML the social scraper fetches — so SPAs need SSR/prerender for correct previews.

questions.question: Core Web Vitals influence SEO because they measure:
questions.explanation: LCP, INP, CLS measure real UX; Google uses them as ranking signals. Use Lighthouse to monitor.

questions.question: How do you get a 2D drawing context from a <canvas>?
questions.explanation: getContext('2d') returns the CanvasRenderingContext2D used for all drawing commands. 'webgl' returns the 3D context.

questions.question: What does ctx.fillRect(10, 10, 100, 50) draw?

options.text: A 100x50 rectangle whose top-left is at (10,10)

questions.explanation: fillRect(x, y, width, height) fills a rectangle from top-left (x,y). Coordinates are in canvas pixels.

questions.question: Canvas drawing is best described as:
questions.explanation: Canvas is immediate-mode: you issue drawing commands that paint pixels to a bitmap. There's no DOM node per shape (unlike SVG).

questions.question: To handle high-DPI (Retina) displays without blurriness you should:

options.text: Set canvas.width = cssWidth * devicePixelRatio and scale the context
Leave it; canvas is always sharp

questions.explanation: Backing store must match physical pixels: width/height = CSS size * devicePixelRatio, then ctx.scale(ratio, ratio) so drawing coords stay CSS-based.

questions.question: Before redrawing a new frame (animation), you typically call:
questions.explanation: clearRect erases a region so old frames don't smear. Forgetting it is a classic canvas bug.

questions.question: Which library renders charts using <canvas> under the hood?
questions.explanation: Chart.js draws on a canvas element for performant 2D charts. D3 typically uses SVG instead.

questions.question: For GPU-accelerated 3D graphics on canvas you use:
questions.explanation: WebGL provides a separate context (getContext('webgl'/'webgl2')) for hardware-accelerated 3D rendering on the canvas bitmap.

questions.question: Performance best practice for canvas is to:

options.text: Batch drawing ops and minimize state changes
Use one draw call per pixel

questions.explanation: Batching and reducing context state changes (fillStyle swaps, etc.) improves throughput; also consider offscreen canvas.

questions.question: Which input type is best for a single on/off binary choice shown as a checkbox?
questions.explanation: checkbox = independent on/off. radio = pick one of many in a group (same name).

questions.question: To constrain a text input to a specific format (e.g. Indian PIN 6 digits) you use:
questions.explanation: The pattern attribute takes a RegExp the value must match for native validation. Combine with title for guidance.

questions.question: type="search" primarily differs from text by:

options.text: Offering a clear ('x') button and semantic role for search

questions.explanation: search inputs render a clear button and carry search semantics; behavior is otherwise similar to text.

questions.question: The 'autocomplete' attribute helps by:

options.text: Hinting the browser how to prefill fields (e.g. autocomplete="email")

questions.explanation: autocomplete provides hints (email, name, street-address) so browsers/password managers prefill correctly — better UX and a11y.

questions.question: Cross-browser inconsistency is most likely with:
questions.explanation: Date/color pickers render as OS-native widgets with varying UIs; test across browsers and have JS fallbacks.

questions.question: Which is a best practice when pairing inputs with labels?

options.text: Wrap input in <label> or use for/id so clicking the label focuses the input
Use placeholder as the only label
Put label after a <div> with no association

questions.explanation: Label association (for/id or wrapping) improves a11y and UX (click target). Placeholders are NOT labels.

questions.question: type="number" with step="0.5" means:
questions.explanation: step controls the increment for spinner/arrow keys and validation granularity.

questions.question: Why still validate on the server even when using type/pattern/min/max?

options.text: Client validation can be bypassed, so server is the source of truth

questions.explanation: All client-side constraints are advisory and bypassable; authoritative checks belong server-side.

questions.question: Shadow Root is best described as:

options.text: A document fragment that is the root of a shadow tree attached to a host

questions.explanation: The shadow root is the root node of the shadow tree; it's attached to the host element and encapsulates content/styles.

questions.question: What is the 'light DOM'?

options.text: The DOM nodes authored by the page author that get slotted into a component

questions.explanation: Light DOM = the regular DOM children you write in markup; they're projected into the shadow tree via <slot>.

questions.question: How do you style light-DOM children from INSIDE the shadow tree?
questions.explanation: ::slotted() targets distributed light-DOM children. You can only style the slot's top-level assigned nodes, not their descendants.

questions.question: A <slot> with no content projected shows its:

options.text: Fallback content (children of the slot element)

questions.explanation: Default/fallback content placed inside <slot> renders when no matching light-DOM child is assigned.

questions.question: CSS custom properties (__var) penetrate shadow boundaries. Why is that useful?

options.text: They let a host theme a component's internals while keeping other styles encapsulated
They only work in closed mode

questions.explanation: CSS variables inherit through shadow boundaries, making them the standard way to expose theming hooks without leaking other styles.

questions.question: Attach a shadow root in JS with:
questions.explanation: attachShadow({mode:'open'|'closed'}) creates and returns the shadow root. open lets element.shadowRoot be read.

questions.question: In Angular, the DEFAULT ViewEncapsulation is:
questions.explanation: Angular defaults to Emulated encapsulation (attribute-scoped selectors) for broad browser support; ShadowDom uses real shadow roots.

questions.question: Event retargeting means a click inside a component is seen by outside listeners as targeting:

options.text: The shadow host element (not internal nodes)

questions.explanation: Retargeting preserves encapsulation: external listeners see the host as the event target, hiding internal structure.

questions.question: The three CORE technologies of Web Components are:

options.text: Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, HTML Templates
CSS, JS, HTML (the standard web trio)

questions.explanation: Web Components are built from Custom Elements (new tags), Shadow DOM (encapsulation), and HTML Templates (<template>/<slot>).

questions.question: Custom Elements are defined with:
questions.explanation: customElements.define(name, class) registers a new tag; the class must extend HTMLElement.

questions.question: Which lifecycle callback runs when a custom element is inserted into the DOM?
questions.explanation: connectedCallback fires on insertion; disconnectedCallback on removal; attributeChangedCallback on observed attr change.

questions.question: To react to attribute changes you must:
questions.explanation: observedAttributes getter lists tracked attributes; attributeChangedCallback then fires on their changes.

questions.question: HTML <template> is used because:

options.text: Its content is inert (not rendered) until cloned into the DOM
It renders immediately like a div

questions.explanation: <template> holds markup that isn't displayed; you clone its .content (DocumentFragment) to instantiate UI repeatedly.

questions.question: Web Components differ from Angular/Vue components in that they:

options.text: Are framework-agnostic standard APIs usable anywhere

questions.explanation: Web Components are native browser standards — no framework required and interoperable across frameworks.

questions.question: A challenge with Web Components in SPAs is:

options.text: Server-side rendering / hydration support is less mature than framework components

questions.explanation: SSR/hydration and advanced tooling (like Angular's DI) integrate less seamlessly with raw Web Components.

questions.question: Angular Material icons often render via:
questions.explanation: mat-icon with svgIcon uses SVG, a common Web Component/icon pattern — scalable and styleable.

questions.question: The srcset attribute lets the browser:

options.text: Choose the best image source from a list based on screen density/size

questions.explanation: srcset provides candidate URLs with width (w) or density (x) descriptors; the browser picks the optimal one.

questions.question: The 'sizes' attribute tells the browser:

options.text: How much layout space the image will occupy, so it can pick the right srcset candidate
The number of images to load

questions.explanation: sizes describes rendered width (e.g. '(max-width:600px) 100vw, 50vw'), letting the browser select the correct srcset source.

questions.question: For 'art direction' (different crop or composition at different widths) you use:
questions.explanation: lets you serve entirely different images per media condition (art direction), with as the fallback.

questions.question: To enable native lazy-loading you add:
questions.explanation: loading="lazy" defers offscreen images until near viewport, improving initial load. Use loading="eager" for above-the-fold.

questions.question: Specifying width and height attributes on helps:

options.text: Reserve space and reduce layout shift (CLS)

questions.explanation: Known dimensions let the browser reserve aspect-ratio space, preventing Cumulative Layout Shift (a Core Web Vital).

questions.question: A modern format fallback strategy uses:
questions.explanation: Serve WebP/AVIF via with a universally-supported fallback for older browsers.

questions.question: x-descriptors in srcset (e.g. image.jpg 2x) describe:

options.text: Device pixel density (DPR) the candidate is intended for

questions.explanation: 1x/2x/3x tell the browser which source matches the device pixel ratio (retina). w-descriptors pair with sizes instead.

questions.question: Providing a descriptive alt attribute is important because:

options.text: It aids accessibility AND can appear if the image fails to load
It is required for srcset to work

questions.explanation: alt supports screen readers and shows as broken-image text; decorative images should use alt="".

questions.question: Which element represents self-contained, distributable content like a blog post or news article?
questions.explanation: <article> = independent, reusable content. <section> groups related content (often with a heading).

questions.question: The 'document outline' is built primarily from:
questions.explanation: A logical h1→h6 hierarchy plus landmark/sectioning elements creates an accessible outline for SR users and SEO.

questions.question: What implicit ARIA role does <aside> map to?
questions.explanation: <aside> → role="complementary" (tangential content like sidebars). <nav>→navigation, <header>→banner.

questions.question: Why should you AVOID skipping heading levels (e.g. h1 then h3)?

options.text: It confuses the document outline and assistive-tech navigation
It is invalid HTML that won't render

questions.explanation: Heading levels should reflect structure; skipping levels misleads SR users who navigate by heading.

questions.question: Landmark elements (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>) help users by:

options.text: Letting AT users jump quickly between page regions

questions.explanation: Landmarks create navigable regions; SR users can jump straight to nav/main/complementary content.

questions.question: <time datetime="2025-01-01T09:00Z"> is useful for:

options.text: Providing a machine-readable date/time to parsers and search engines

questions.explanation: The datetime attribute gives a standardized value while the element shows human text — great for events/SEO.

questions.question: A common semantic mistake is:

options.text: Using <div> for everything instead of meaningful landmarks

questions.explanation: Overusing generic divs instead of semantic/landmark elements harms accessibility and SEO.

questions.question: Compared to ARIA, semantic HTML is preferred because it:

options.text: Provides built-in roles/states with less risk and better browser support

questions.explanation: Native semantics are robust and need no extra attributes; ARIA is the fallback for gaps (first rule of ARIA).

questions.question: HTML5 provides validation via attributes such as:

options.text: required, min, max, minlength, maxlength, pattern, type

questions.explanation: Native constraints: required, min/max (numbers/dates), minlength/maxlength, pattern (regex), and type-based checks (email/url).

questions.question: The :invalid CSS pseudo-class targets:

options.text: Inputs whose current value fails a constraint

questions.explanation: :invalid styles fields that currently violate a constraint (e.g. empty required). Pair with :valid for feedback UI.

questions.question: To show a custom validation message you use the Constraint Validation API:
questions.explanation: setCustomValidity('') clears (valid); a non-empty string marks invalid and reportValidity() shows the bubble.

questions.question: The 'pattern' attribute uses:

options.text: A JavaScript-style regular expression the value must match

questions.explanation: pattern holds a RegExp (anchored automatically); it's evaluated against the value during validation. Add title for guidance.

questions.question: novalidate on a <form> does what?

options.text: Disables native browser validation for that form

questions.explanation: novalidate turns off built-in validation — useful when you handle validation entirely in JS.

questions.question: An edge case with pattern: the regex is implicitly:

options.text: Anchored (must match the whole value), so ^ and $ are not needed

questions.explanation: HTML pattern validation anchors the regex to the full value; you don't add ^...$. A partial match fails.

questions.question: In Angular Reactive Forms, validators like Validators.email are set:

options.text: In the FormControl/FormGroup definition (component), not the template

questions.explanation: Reactive Forms define Validators in TS (e.g. this.fb.group({email:[null, Validators.email]})), keeping logic in code.

questions.question: Best practice: validate on BOTH client and server because:

options.text: Client validation is for UX; server validation is the authoritative security check
Server validation is slower so skip it
Only one layer is ever needed

questions.explanation: Client-side gives instant feedback; server-side is mandatory because client checks are bypassable.

questions.question: Flexbox is best for which kind of layout?

options.text: One-dimensional (a single row OR column) alignment
Two-dimensional grid layouts with rows AND columns

questions.explanation: Flexbox is one-dimensional (main axis only). For 2D row+column layouts, CSS Grid is the better tool.

questions.question: justify-content controls alignment along the:

options.text: Main axis (the direction set by flex-direction)

questions.explanation: justify-content = main-axis distribution (start/center/space-between...). align-items = cross-axis.

questions.question: To vertically AND horizontally center a single child you use:
questions.explanation: Flex centering needs both axes: justify-content (main) + align-items (cross). This is the classic centering trick.

questions.question: flex: 1 is shorthand for:
questions.explanation: flex:1 = grow 1, shrink 1, basis 0% — items share free space equally. A common equal-width pattern.

questions.question: flex-basis defines:

options.text: The initial main-size of an item before grow/shrink is applied

questions.explanation: flex-basis sets the starting size along the main axis; grow/shrink then adjust it relative to free space.

questions.question: To prevent a flex item from shrinking below its content you set:
questions.explanation: flex-shrink:0 stops the item from shrinking. Useful for icons/buttons you want to keep at natural size.

questions.question: flex-wrap: wrap allows items to:

options.text: Flow onto multiple lines when they don't fit

questions.explanation: wrap lets flex items break to new lines instead of overflowing; align-content then controls spacing of those lines.

questions.question: A common mistake is:

options.text: Using flexbox for full 2D page grids instead of CSS Grid

questions.explanation: Flexbox is 1D; forcing it into complex 2D layouts gets awkward. Reach for Grid for 2D, flex for 1D alignment.

questions.question: CSS Grid is primarily used for:
questions.explanation: Grid excels at 2D layouts; Flexbox is for 1D. Choose based on whether you need row+column control.

questions.question: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) does what?

options.text: Creates as many 200px-min columns as fit, stretching them to fill (responsive)
Sets a fixed 200px width regardless of screen

questions.explanation: auto-fit + minmax is the classic responsive grid: columns auto-flow to fill width, each at least 200px.

questions.question: The 'fr' unit represents:

options.text: A fraction of the available grid space

questions.explanation: 1fr = one share of leftover space. Used to distribute tracks proportionally after fixed sizes are accounted for.

questions.question: To place an item in a specific area you can use:
questions.explanation: Grid items are placed via line-based (grid-column: 1 / 3) or named areas (grid-template-areas).

questions.question: gap in grid controls:

options.text: The spacing between rows and columns

questions.explanation: gap (row-gap/column-gap) sets gutters between tracks without margins — cleaner than margin hacks.

questions.question: grid-template-areas lets you:

options.text: Name regions in a visual ASCII-like layout and assign items to them

questions.explanation: grid-template-areas uses named cells ('header header' / 'sidebar main') for intuitive, readable layouts.

questions.question: Which is TRUE about Grid vs Flexbox?
questions.explanation: The key mental model: Grid = 2D (both axes at once), Flex = 1D (content-driven along one axis).

questions.question: justify-items vs justify-content in grid differ because:

options.text: justify-items aligns items INSIDE their cells; justify-content aligns the grid TRACKS in the container

questions.explanation: justify-items positions items within their grid area; justify-content positions the whole grid when it's narrower than the container.

questions.question: position: absolute removes an element from normal flow and positions it relative to:

options.text: Its nearest positioned ancestor (or the viewport if none)

questions.explanation: absolute is offset from the nearest ancestor with position != static. Without one, it falls back to the initial containing block (viewport).

questions.question: position: fixed differs from absolute because it is relative to:
questions.explanation: fixed positions relative to the viewport and doesn't move on scroll (great for headers/modals).

questions.question: position: sticky behaves like:

options.text: relative until it would scroll past a threshold, then sticks like fixed within its parent

questions.explanation: sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll position, constrained to its containing block — perfect for sticky headers.

questions.question: For position: absolute/relative/fixed, the offsets (top/right/bottom/left) are ignored when:
questions.explanation: top/left/etc. only apply to positioned elements (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky). With static they're ignored.

questions.question: z-index controls:

options.text: Stacking order of positioned elements (which appears on top)

questions.explanation: z-index sets paint order among positioned elements within the same stacking context; higher = closer to viewer.

questions.question: A 'stacking context' is created by, among others:

options.text: position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, will-change, flex/grid child with z-index

questions.explanation: Many properties create a new stacking context (transform, opacity, position+z-index, will-change...), scoping z-index locally.

questions.question: To center an absolutely-positioned box both ways you use:
questions.explanation: Offset to 50% then translate back by half its own size — the classic absolute-centering technique.

questions.question: When is absolute positioning a poor choice?

options.text: For whole page layout (it breaks document flow and responsive behavior)

questions.explanation: Absolute positioning yanks elements from flow; using it for major layouts harms responsiveness. Flex/Grid are better for layout.

questions.question: Which selector matches a <button> element with class 'primary'?
questions.explanation: button.primary = element type AND class. .primary button (descendant) and button#primary (ID) are different.

questions.question: The child combinator '>' selects:
questions.explanation: ul > li matches li's that are direct children of ul. The space (descendant) combinator matches any depth.

questions.question: a:hover, a:focus, a:active are examples of:
questions.explanation: Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :nth-child) target states/positions. Pseudo-elements (::before) target parts of an element.

questions.question: input[type="text"] is an:
questions.explanation: Square brackets denote attribute selectors; they match elements by attribute presence/value.

questions.question: p::first-line targets:

options.text: The first formatted line of a paragraph (a pseudo-element)

questions.explanation: ::first-line (double-colon) is a pseudo-element styling the first line. ::first-letter targets the first character.

questions.question: The universal selector is written as:
questions.explanation: * matches any element. It has the lowest specificity (0,0,0,0) and is often used in resets (e.g. * { box-sizing }).

questions.question: li:nth-child(2n) selects:

options.text: Every even-positioned li among its siblings

questions.explanation: :nth-child(2n) = even positions (2nd, 4th...). :nth-child(2) would be only the 2nd. Useful for zebra striping.

questions.question: Which has HIGHER specificity: '.nav li a' or 'header a'?
questions.explanation: Specificity counts (IDs, classes, elements). '.nav li a' has 1 class + 2 elements vs 'header a' 0 classes + 2 elements.

questions.question: The specificity tiers, highest to lowest, are:
questions.explanation: Specificity order: inline (1,0,0,0) > ID (0,1,0,0) > class/attr/pseudo-class (0,0,1,0) > element/pseudo-element (0,0,0,1).

questions.question: For an element with id='main' class='error' and inline style color:green, which color wins?
questions.explanation: Inline styles have the highest specificity (1,0,0,0) and beat ID/class/element selectors (unless !important is involved).

questions.question: When two rules have EQUAL specificity, which wins?

options.text: The one defined LATER in the source order

questions.explanation: Source order is the tie-breaker: among equal-specificity rules, the last-declared wins.

questions.question: How does !important affect resolution?

options.text: It overrides normal declarations (including inline), except another !important later

questions.explanation: !important beats non-important rules (even inline). Among !important rules, normal specificity/source order then apply.

questions.question: The :not() pseudo-class contributes specificity equal to:

options.text: The specificity of the selector INSIDE it

questions.explanation: p:not(.intro) has specificity of p (0,0,0,1) PLUS .intro (0,0,1,0) = 0,0,1,1. :not itself adds nothing; its argument does.

questions.question: A common best practice to avoid 'specificity wars' is:

options.text: Keep selectors low-specificity and use BEM naming

questions.explanation: Low-specificity selectors + BEM reduce conflicts so you don't escalate with IDs/!important. Override third-party styles by raising specificity, not !important.

questions.question: Which selector is most specific: '#nav .item a', '.nav a', 'nav a', '* a'?
questions.explanation: IDs weigh the most. '#nav .item a' includes an ID so it beats class- and element-only selectors.

questions.question: Specificity differs from the cascade in that:

options.text: Specificity picks the winning rule among matches; the cascade is the WHOLE algorithm (origin, importance, specificity, order)
They are the exact same thing

questions.explanation: The cascade is the full process (importance/origin → specificity → source order). Specificity is just one step within it.

questions.question: The CSS 'cascade' refers to:

options.text: The algorithm that resolves which declarations apply when multiple rules match

questions.explanation: The cascade combines origin/importance, specificity, and source order to decide the winning value for each property.

questions.question: The cascade resolution order starts with:

options.text: Origin & importance (e.g. user !important vs author vs UA styles)

questions.explanation: Step 1 is origin/importance (user-agent < author < author !important < user !important). Specificity/order come later.

questions.question: User-agent (browser default) styles are overridden by:

options.text: Author stylesheets (your CSS) in normal cases

questions.explanation: Author (website) styles normally beat UA defaults. Resets/normalizers exist precisely to override UA inconsistencies.

questions.question: What does the 'inherit' keyword do for a property?

options.text: Forces the value to be taken from the parent element

questions.explanation: inherit explicitly takes the parent's computed value. Some properties (color, font-family) inherit automatically; others don't.

questions.question: The 'initial' keyword sets a property to:

options.text: Its CSS specification-defined initial value (not the UA style)

questions.explanation: initial resets to the property's defined initial value per spec (e.g. color: initial = black), distinct from the browser default look.

questions.question: Two rules with identical specificity and origin — the winner is decided by:
questions.explanation: After origin/importance and specificity are equal, the cascade falls back to source order: last declaration wins.

questions.question: Why is understanding the cascade important in large apps (e.g. Angular)?

options.text: To predictably override third-party/component styles without !important sprawl
It only matters for print media

questions.explanation: With many layers (libs, components, themes), the cascade explains why a style wins; raise specificity intentionally rather than spray !important.

questions.question: The 'revert' keyword (vs initial/unset) means:

options.text: Roll back to the value the cascade would have had without the current author rule (UA or inherited)

questions.explanation: revert undoes the author-level change, falling back to UA style or inherited value (depending on the property) — smarter than initial.

questions.question: A CSS @keyframes animation is defined and then applied with:
questions.explanation: You declare @keyframes name {...} then use animation: name 2s ... (or longhands) to run it. Transitions are a different mechanism.

questions.question: The difference between animation and transition is:

options.text: Animations have multiple keyframes & loop/auto-run; transitions animate BETWEEN two states on a change

questions.explanation: Transitions interpolate from one state to another when a property changes. Animations run a keyframe sequence, can loop and auto-start.

questions.question: animation-iteration-count: infinite makes the animation:
questions.explanation: iteration-count sets repeat count; infinite loops endlessly. Pair with animation-direction for alternate ping-pong.

questions.question: For smooth, performant animations you should prefer animating:
questions.explanation: transform/opacity are handled on the compositor (GPU) and avoid layout/paint. Animating layout properties (width/top) triggers reflow — janky.

questions.question: animation-fill-mode: forwards keeps:

options.text: The values of the LAST keyframe applied after the animation ends
The values of the FIRST keyframe

questions.explanation: fill-mode: forwards retains the end state post-animation; without it the element snaps back to its pre-animation style.

questions.question: To start an animation only after a delay you use:
questions.explanation: animation-delay postpones the start. (transition-delay is for transitions, not keyframe animations.)

questions.question: 0% and 100% in @keyframes are equivalent to:
questions.explanation: @keyframes { from {...} to {...} } is shorthand for 0% and 100%. You can add intermediate % steps.

questions.question: prefers-reduced-motion is important because:

options.text: It lets you disable/reduce motion for users who get motion sickness (accessibility)
It is required for animations to run

questions.explanation: Respect prefers-reduced-motion: reduce to minimize animation for vestibular-sensitive users — an a11y best practice.

questions.question: A transition animates:

options.text: A property's value change BETWEEN two states when it occurs

questions.explanation: Transitions interpolate when a property changes (e.g. :hover). For keyframe sequences, use animations.

questions.question: The minimum needed to see a transition is:
questions.explanation: Without a duration (default 0s) the change is instant. You need both the property to watch and a non-zero duration.

questions.question: transition: all 0.3s ease; will:

options.text: Animate all transitionable properties over 0.3s with ease timing

questions.explanation: Shorthand: transition: <property> <duration> <timing-function> <delay>. 'all' targets every animatable property (use specific props to avoid surprises).

questions.question: transition-timing-function: ease-in-out controls:

options.text: The acceleration curve (slow-fast-slow) of the transition
The number of times it repeats

questions.explanation: Timing functions (ease, linear, ease-in-out, cubic-bezier) shape the progress over time, not the duration/delay.

questions.question: A property will NOT transition if:

options.text: It has no intermediate computed value (e.g. display: none → block)

questions.explanation: Transitions need interpolatable values. display can't tween, so use opacity/visibility/transform for show-hide effects.

questions.question: Transitions vs animations: which can auto-run on page load without a state change?

options.text: Animations (keyframes auto-run); transitions need a trigger
Transitions auto-run; animations need a trigger

questions.explanation: Animations start automatically (or via animation-play-state). Transitions only fire when a property actually changes.

questions.question: transition-delay: 0.5s means:

options.text: The transition begins 0.5s AFTER the property change

questions.explanation: Delay postpones the start; duration (separate) sets how long the tween lasts.

questions.question: Good practice for hover transitions is:

options.text: Define the transition on the BASE state so both enter AND leave are smooth

questions.explanation: Putting transition on the base element means leaving :hover also animates back. Defining only on :hover makes the exit instant.

questions.question: Responsive design means a site:

options.text: Adapts layout/content to different screen sizes and devices
Requires a separate mobile domain only

questions.explanation: Responsive design fluidly adapts via fluid grids, flexible media, and media queries — one codebase for all devices.

questions.question: The viewport meta tag <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width"> does:

options.text: Tells mobile browsers to use the device width (not a zoomed-out 980px default)

questions.explanation: Without it, mobile renders at ~980px and scales down. width=device-width makes CSS media queries match the real device width.

questions.question: Mobile-first design means:

options.text: Write base styles for small screens, then enhance for larger via min-width media queries

questions.explanation: Mobile-first: default = mobile styles; min-width queries add layout as the viewport grows. Often improves performance (less override).

questions.question: Fluid typography can use:

options.text: clamp(min, preferred, max) for responsive font sizes

questions.explanation: clamp() gives a fluid size bounded between min and max (e.g. clamp(1rem, 2vw + 1rem, 1.5rem)) — great for responsive type.

questions.question: Relative units like % and fr help responsiveness because they:

options.text: Scale with their container/viewport instead of fixed pixels

questions.explanation: Fluid units (% , vw, fr, em) adapt to context; fixed px does not. This is core to fluid grids.

questions.question: A responsive image strategy includes:
questions.explanation: Serve right-sized images per device via srcset/sizes and art-direction via <picture> to save bandwidth and improve LCP.

questions.question: Common breakpoints are chosen based on:

options.text: Real device/content needs, not just 'phone/tablet/desktop' labels

questions.explanation: Design by where your layout breaks, using content-driven breakpoints — avoid rigid device-class assumptions.

questions.question: Which helps a layout reflow from multi-column to single-column on small screens?

options.text: Flex wrap or Grid auto-fit/minmax with a max-width media query

questions.explanation: Flex wrap or Grid's auto-fit/minmax naturally collapse to fewer columns; media queries can force single-column past a breakpoint.

questions.question: A media query @media (max-width: 600px) applies when:

options.text: The viewport width is 600px or LESS
The viewport width is 600px or MORE
The device is a tablet only

questions.explanation: max-width: N matches viewports ≤ N. min-width: N matches ≥ N (used in mobile-first).

questions.question: In a mobile-first approach you use:

options.text: min-width media queries (enhance as screen grows)

questions.explanation: Mobile-first base styles target small screens; min-width queries layer on larger layouts.

questions.question: You can query features beyond width, such as:
questions.explanation: @media supports orientation, hover capability, prefers-color-scheme (dark mode), prefers-reduced-motion, etc.

questions.question: prefers-color-scheme: dark lets you:

options.text: Apply a dark theme when the user's OS is in dark mode

questions.explanation: Respect OS theme preference to auto-switch light/dark — great UX and accessibility win.

questions.question: Combining conditions: @media (min-width: 600px) and (max-width: 900px) matches:
questions.explanation: The 'and' operator requires ALL conditions true — a bounded range (common tablet breakpoint).

questions.question: A 'logical' media query with 'or' uses:

options.text: A comma (,) between queries — any matching query applies

questions.explanation: Commas separate queries as alternatives (like OR). 'and' requires all; ',' requires any.

questions.question: Why avoid too many fixed breakpoints?

options.text: They create maintenance burden and may not match real device needs

questions.explanation: Fewer, content-driven breakpoints (often via fluid techniques) are easier to maintain and more robust than many rigid ones.

questions.question: @media print is used to:

options.text: Style how a page looks when printed (hide nav, show URLs)

questions.explanation: Print media queries optimize printed output — hide chrome, expand links, set page margins.

questions.question: Container queries let a component respond to:

options.text: The size of its CONTAINER, not the viewport

questions.explanation: Unlike media queries (viewport-based), container queries adapt a component to its parent's width — true component-driven responsiveness.

questions.question: Before a container query can target an element, you must:

options.text: Set container-type: inline-size (or size) on an ANCESTOR

questions.explanation: container-type establishes an element as a query container; @container then queries its size. The query container is the ancestor, not the element itself.

questions.question: The syntax to apply styles based on container width is:
questions.explanation: @container queries the nearest ancestor container. This is the modern replacement for hacky viewport-based component styling.

questions.question: The main advantage over media queries is:

options.text: A component restyles correctly wherever it's placed (sidebar, main, card) without knowing the viewport

questions.explanation: Components become self-adapting to their context, enabling true reusable UI — a big win for design systems.

questions.question: container-type: inline-size vs size differs in that:

options.text: inline-size queries only the inline (width) axis; size allows both dimensions but blocks size containment

questions.explanation: inline-size (most common) containers query width cheaply. size enables block-axis queries but applies size containment (children can't affect container size).

questions.question: Can you name a container for targeted queries?
questions.explanation: container-name lets you scope @container to a named container, useful when multiple containers exist.

questions.question: Container queries are especially valuable for:

options.text: Reusable design-system components placed in varying layouts

questions.explanation: Components (cards, widgets) that appear in sidebars, grids, and modals benefit most — they adapt to placement, not viewport.

questions.question: For older browsers without support, you should:

options.text: Provide a sensible default (viewport media query / base styles) as fallback

questions.explanation: Progressive enhancement: default layout works without container queries; @supports can gate advanced styling.

questions.question: BEM stands for:
questions.explanation: BEM is a naming methodology: Block (component), Element (part of block, __), Modifier (variant, --).

questions.question: The BEM class for a 'button' inside a 'card' block, in a 'primary' variant:
questions.explanation: block__element--modifier: card (block) + __button (element) + --primary (modifier). Single class per node, flat specificity.

questions.question: A key benefit of BEM is:

options.text: Flat, predictable specificity (single-class selectors) and self-documenting structure

questions.explanation: BEM uses one class per element, so specificity stays (0,0,1,0) — avoids specificity wars and makes styles portable.

questions.question: In BEM, an Element is denoted by:
questions.explanation: Elements use block__element. Modifiers use --, blocks stand alone. This keeps the three-part convention clear.

questions.question: A Modifier represents:

options.text: A state or variant of a block/element (e.g. disabled, large, theme)

questions.explanation: Modifiers (--primary, --disabled) flag variations without creating new blocks — keep base styles and extend.

questions.question: Why avoid nesting BEM elements like block__el1__el2?

options.text: It breaks the block/element model; elements belong to the block, not other elements

questions.explanation: BEM elements are flat: block__child, not block__parent__child. Deep nesting couples styles to structure.

questions.question: BEM helps avoid specificity issues because it encourages:
questions.explanation: Each node gets one class → specificity is always (0,0,1,0). Predictable overrides without escalating selectors.

questions.question: In a component framework (Angular), BEM pairs well because:

options.text: Component-scoped templates map cleanly to blocks, keeping styles readable and conflict-free

questions.explanation: BEM's block = component mental model; combined with framework view encapsulation, styles stay modular and clear.

questions.question: CSS custom properties (variables) are declared as:
questions.explanation: Custom properties use the --name syntax. $ is Sass; var() is how you READ a variable, not declare it.

questions.question: You consume a variable with:
questions.explanation: var(--name) reads the custom property. You can supply a fallback: var(--x, #000).

questions.question: A key advantage of CSS variables over preprocessor vars is:

options.text: They are runtime/live — can change via JS and respond to media queries/state

questions.explanation: CSS vars are live in the browser: update via element.style or :root, animate, and react to themes — unlike static preprocessor constants.

questions.question: Defining --brand on :root makes it:
questions.explanation: :root is the document root; a variable declared there is inherited everywhere — the standard place for theme tokens.

questions.question: CSS variables CASCADE and are:

options.text: Inherited — a child inherits the value from its parent unless overridden

questions.explanation: Custom properties inherit like color/font-family. This enables theming: set --brand on a container, all descendants use it.

questions.question: You can update a CSS variable from JavaScript via:
questions.explanation: setProperty('--name', value) updates a custom property live — great for themes, sliders, and dynamic styling.

questions.question: A common use for CSS variables is:

options.text: Centralized design tokens (colors, spacing, radii) and theming (light/dark)

questions.explanation: Tokens + theming are the canonical use: switch a few root vars to re-skin the whole app (incl. dark mode).

questions.question: A fallback value is written as:
questions.explanation: The second argument to var() is the fallback used when the variable is not defined (or invalid).

questions.question: Tailwind CSS is best described as:

options.text: A utility-first CSS framework (compose styles via small classes like p-4, flex)
A component library with prebuilt buttons

questions.explanation: Tailwind is utility-first: you build UIs by applying atomic classes (flex, p-4, text-sm) directly in markup.

questions.question: The JIT engine (Tailwind v3+) does:

options.text: Generates only the CSS for classes actually used in your markup
Loads all possible classes upfront (massive file)

questions.explanation: JIT scans content files and emits just the used utilities, keeping the bundle tiny and enabling arbitrary values (e.g. w-[330px]).

questions.question: Responsive variants use a prefix like:
