options.text: md:flex, lg:grid (breakpoint prefix before the utility)

questions.explanation: Breakpoint prefixes (sm:, md:, lg:) apply utilities at min-width breakpoints — mobile-first.

questions.question: Customization (colors, spacing) is done in:
questions.explanation: tailwind.config.js defines content paths and theme.extend tokens; the engine reads it to generate utilities.

questions.question: A downside of utility classes is:

options.text: Markup can become verbose / harder to read for complex components

questions.explanation: Verbose class strings are the common critique; mitigated by @apply, components, and frameworks (Angular/React) extracting repeated patterns.

questions.question: To reuse a group of utilities as a component you can use:

options.text: @apply in CSS or extract a component class/template

questions.explanation: @apply composes utilities into a custom class; or build a component so the class list lives in one place.

questions.question: Arbitrary values are written as:
questions.explanation: JIT supports arbitrary values in brackets for one-off needs without editing the config.

questions.question: Tailwind differs from BEM in that:

options.text: Tailwind uses utility classes in markup; BEM uses semantic, single-class names in stylesheets

questions.explanation: Tailwind = utility classes in HTML; BEM = semantic naming in CSS. They address styling differently (composition vs naming).

questions.question: CSS architecture aims to solve:

options.text: Scalability, maintainability, and avoiding style conflicts in large codebases

questions.explanation: As projects grow, ad-hoc CSS becomes unmaintainable; architecture (BEM, ITCSS, modules) brings order and predictability.

questions.question: ITCSS (Inverted Triangle CSS) organizes styles by:

options.text: Specificity/layer — from generic (settings, tools) to specific (components, trumps)

questions.explanation: ITCSS layers from low- to high-specificity (settings→tools→generic→elements→objects→components→utilities) to control the cascade.

questions.question: CSS Modules (in build tooling) provide:

options.text: Locally-scoped class names to avoid global collisions

questions.explanation: CSS Modules hash/namespace class names per file, preventing accidental cross-file clashes in component-based apps.

questions.question: A 'reset' (e.g. normalize.css) primarily:

options.text: Reduces cross-browser inconsistencies in default styles

questions.explanation: Resets/normalizers even out UA defaults so layouts start from a consistent baseline across browsers.

questions.question: Good architecture keeps specificity:

options.text: Low and flat so overrides are predictable (avoid deep selectors/IDs)
As high as possible with IDs
Equal to the number of files

questions.explanation: Low-specificity, single-class selectors keep the cascade predictable and reduce the need for !important.

questions.question: In Angular, component ViewEncapsulation helps architecture by:

options.text: Scoping component styles so they don't leak globally

questions.explanation: Encapsulation scopes styles per component (Emulated by default), a built-in architectural boundary that reduces leaks.

questions.question: The 'utility-first' architecture (Tailwind) trades:

options.text: Semantic class names for composable utility classes in markup

questions.explanation: Utility-first moves styling into atomic classes rather than bespoke semantic classes — different tradeoff vs BEM-style architecture.

questions.question: A maintainable large-scale approach often combines:

options.text: Design tokens (variables) + BEM/Modules + a layering strategy

questions.explanation: Tokens for theming, a naming/scoping convention, and disciplined layering together keep CSS scalable.

questions.question: display: grid on a container makes its direct children:

options.text: Grid items laid out along defined rows and columns

questions.explanation: grid establishes a grid formatting context; direct children become grid items placed into the implicit/explicit tracks.

questions.question: grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr creates:

options.text: Three columns where the middle takes twice the free space of the outer two

questions.explanation: fr units share leftover space proportionally: 2fr gets double the 1fr columns' share.

questions.question: The 'implicit grid' is created when:

options.text: Items are placed beyond the explicitly defined rows/columns

questions.explanation: Explicit tracks come from template-*; auto-placed items that overflow generate implicit rows/columns (sized by grid-auto-rows/columns).

questions.question: To make a 12-column layout where an item spans columns 2-9, use:
questions.explanation: grid-column: start / end uses line numbers (end is exclusive). 2/10 spans lines 2 through 9 = 7 columns.

questions.question: grid-auto-flow: dense helps by:

options.text: Backfilling earlier gaps with smaller items to reduce holes

questions.explanation: dense packing reorders auto-placement to fill gaps, producing a tighter layout (at the cost of source order).

questions.question: minmax(100px, 1fr) as a track size means:

options.text: At least 100px, but can grow to fill 1fr of free space

questions.explanation: minmax(min, max) sets a flexible range — min(100px) ensures a floor, 1fr lets it expand.

questions.question: place-items: center centers:

options.text: Each grid item within its OWN cell (shorthand for justify/align-items)
The whole grid in the page

questions.explanation: place-items sets both align-items and justify-items, centering content inside each cell — handy for card centers.

questions.question: Subgrid (modern CSS) allows a grid item to:

options.text: Align its OWN children to the parent grid's tracks

questions.explanation: Subgrid lets a nested grid inherit the parent's row/column lines so inner content aligns to the outer layout — great for cards.

questions.question: align-content controls:

options.text: Distribution of FLEX LINES (rows) when there's extra cross-axis space and wrapping

questions.explanation: align-content only matters with flex-wrap and multiple lines; it spaces the lines themselves along the cross axis.

questions.question: align-self overrides for a single item the container's:

options.text: align-items (cross-axis alignment of that one item)

questions.explanation: align-self lets one item opt out of the container's align-items, e.g. push one card to flex-end.

questions.question: order: -1 on a flex item:

options.text: Moves it earlier in the visual order (before items with default order 0)

questions.explanation: order changes visual placement without HTML reordering; negative values sort before 0. Use sparingly for a11y (source order stays).

questions.question: A flex item's automatic minimum size can cause overflow because:

options.text: flex items have min-width:auto by default, refusing to shrink below content size

questions.explanation: min-width:auto means an item won't shrink below its content; set min-width:0 to allow shrinking (fixes common flex overflow bugs).

questions.question: flex: 0 1 auto (the initial value) means:

options.text: Don't grow, allow shrink, basis = content/auto size

questions.explanation: Default flex: 0 1 auto → won't grow to fill, can shrink, starts at auto size. flex:1 (1 1 0%) is the equal-share variant.

questions.question: To create a sticky footer with flexbox you set the container:

options.text: min-height:100vh; display:flex; flex-direction:column; and main { flex:1 }

questions.explanation: A column flex container at full viewport height, with the main region growing (flex:1), pushes the footer down.

questions.question: flex-direction: column-reverse reverses:

options.text: The main axis (items flow bottom-to-top); cross-axis alignment unaffected

questions.explanation: *-reverse flips the main axis direction only; justify-content then applies reversed. align-items stays the same axis.

questions.question: A common pitfall: nesting many flex containers can:

options.text: Complicate layout debugging and stretch performance if overused

questions.explanation: Deep flex nesting is hard to reason about; prefer Grid for 2D and reserve flex for 1D alignment. Use containment for perf.

questions.question: animation-direction: alternate makes the animation:

options.text: Play forward then backward on alternate iterations

questions.explanation: With iteration-count > 1, alternate reverses direction each cycle — ideal for ping-pong/yo-yo effects.

questions.question: animation-play-state: paused is useful for:

options.text: Pausing/resuming via hover or JS without restarting

questions.explanation: Toggling play-state pauses/resumes in place — common for hover-to-pause or scroll-based control.

questions.question: step-end (steps) timing creates:

options.text: Discrete jumps with no interpolation (e.g. sprite frames)

questions.explanation: steps() divides the animation into equal intervals with no tweening between — perfect for sprite animation or tick effects.

questions.question: The will-change property:

options.text: Hints the browser to prepare for an upcoming change (e.g. transform) for smoother animation

questions.explanation: will-change (e.g. will-change: transform) lets the browser promote a layer ahead of time. Use sparingly — overuse wastes memory.

questions.question: Animating 'left'/'top' is generally worse than transform because:

options.text: It triggers layout (reflow) on every frame instead of cheap compositing

questions.explanation: Position changes cause reflow; transform/opacity run on the compositor. Animate transform: translate() instead of top/left.

questions.question: A keyframe at 50% with no 0%/100% still works because:

options.text: The browser uses the element's current computed value for the missing 0% and 100%

questions.explanation: Missing 0%/100% keyframes are synthesized from the element's existing styles, so partial keyframes interpolate from the base.

questions.question: To run two animations on one element:
questions.explanation: animation is a list; comma-separate multiple values to run several animations with independent timing.

questions.question: Best accessibility practice for non-essential animation is:

options.text: Wrap it in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to disable/reduce it

questions.explanation: Respecting reduced-motion prevents discomfort for vestibular-sensitive users — an essential a11y step.

questions.question: Transitioning a property requires the property to be:
questions.explanation: Only animatable properties interpolate. display, position, and visibility aren't (use opacity/transform instead).

questions.question: transition-property: transform, opacity means:

options.text: Only those two properties will animate on change

questions.explanation: List the specific properties to transition; others change instantly. 'all' targets everything (can cause unintended transitions).

questions.question: If you change a property WITHOUT a transition declared, it:
questions.explanation: Transitions only interpolate when a transition is set for that property and a duration > 0; otherwise the change is immediate.

questions.question: A transition defined ONLY on :hover will:

options.text: Animate IN on hover, but snap back instantly when unhovered

questions.explanation: The transition must exist on the base state to also animate the return; otherwise only the hover-in tween occurs.

questions.question: transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) is a:

options.text: Custom easing curve defined by 4 control values

questions.explanation: cubic-bezier lets you craft precise easing (this one is the common 'standard' material curve).

questions.question: Multiple transitions with different durations use:
questions.explanation: transition: color .3s, transform .6s applies per-property timing via comma lists aligned to transition-property.

questions.question: Transitions are commonly triggered by:

options.text: State changes like :hover, :focus, class toggles, or attribute changes

questions.explanation: Any change to a transitioned property value triggers the tween — typically via pseudo-classes or JS-toggled classes.

questions.question: For a reveal effect you should animate:

options.text: opacity and transform (not display/visibility) for smoothness

questions.explanation: display can't tween; fade with opacity and slide with transform, toggling visibility/opacity for accessibility.

questions.question: The general sibling combinator '~' selects:

options.text: All following siblings (not just adjacent) matching the selector

questions.explanation: ~ targets later siblings; + is adjacent-only. Both require the element to follow the reference in the same parent.

questions.question: input:not([disabled]) selects:

options.text: All input elements WITHOUT the disabled attribute

questions.explanation: :not() negates a selector; here it excludes disabled inputs — handy for styling active form fields.

questions.question: A combinator list 'ul li' (space) means:

options.text: Any li that is a DESCENDANT of a ul (any depth)
ul that is a child of li

questions.explanation: The descendant combinator (space) matches any nested level. Use '>' for direct children only.

questions.question: Which selector has the LOWEST specificity?
questions.explanation: Universal * has zero specificity. IDs are highest among these; classes beat elements.

questions.question: a[href^='https'] targets links whose href:
questions.explanation: ^= starts-with, $= ends-with, *= contains. Useful to style external vs internal links.

questions.question: :is() (formerly :any) is useful because it:

options.text: Groups selectors and takes the SPECIFICITY OF ITS MOST SPECIFIC ARGUMENT

questions.explanation: :is(h1,h2,h3) simplifies grouping; its specificity equals the strongest inner selector (unlike :where which is 0).

questions.question: :where() differs from :is() in that it:

options.text: Always has ZERO specificity (great for reset-like rules)

questions.explanation: :where() zero-specificity makes grouped selectors easy to override later — ideal for base/resets without raising specificity.

questions.question: ::before and ::after create:

options.text: Generated content boxes as the first/last child of the selected element

questions.explanation: Pseudo-elements inject decorative content via content:''; require content (even empty) to render. Double-colon is modern syntax.

questions.question: Custom properties are CASE-:
questions.explanation: Custom property names are case-sensitive, unlike many CSS properties. --color and --Color are distinct.

questions.question: A variable's value can include:

options.text: Any valid CSS value, even another var() reference

questions.explanation: Values are substituted as-is; you can nest var() (e.g. --gutter: calc(var(--space) * 2)).

questions.question: Scoping a variable on a specific component (e.g. .card { --accent: red }) means:

options.text: It (and descendants) see --accent:red, but siblings outside don't

questions.explanation: Variables inherit; defining one on .card scopes it to that subtree — the basis for component theming.

questions.question: To enable a dark theme you can:

options.text: Redefine --bg/--text etc. under a [data-theme='dark'] or .dark selector

questions.explanation: Theming via root variables swapped by a theme attribute/Сlass is the standard, low-effort dark-mode technique.

questions.question: calc() with a variable: calc(var(--space) * 2) is:

options.text: Valid and commonly used to derive sizes from tokens

questions.explanation: calc() composes variables for spacing scales, fluid sizes, etc. — a core design-token technique.

questions.question: Invalid variable substitution falls back to:

options.text: The declared fallback in var(--x, fallback), else the property's initial/inherited value

questions.explanation: If a var is invalid/undefined and no fallback given, the property uses its inherited or initial value (not an error).

questions.question: Unlike Sass variables, CSS variables:

options.text: Are resolved in the browser at computed-value time (live, cascade-aware)
Are resolved at build time only

questions.explanation: Sass vars are compile-time constants; CSS custom properties are real, live, cascade-inherited browser values.

questions.question: Reading a variable in JavaScript for computation requires:

options.text: CSS cannot be read by JS

questions.explanation: getComputedStyle returns the resolved custom property value (often with leading whitespace — trim it).

questions.question: The four-part specificity tuple (a,b,c,d) maps to:
questions.explanation: Standard order: inline styles, then IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then elements/pseudo-elements.

questions.question: An attribute selector [type='text'] has specificity equal to:
questions.explanation: Attributes and pseudo-classes sit in the class tier (0,0,1,0) — higher than elements but below IDs.

questions.question: Two competing rules, one .a.b (0,0,2,0) and one #c .d (0,1,1,0): which wins?

options.text: #c .d (it has an ID, so it wins regardless of class count)

questions.explanation: IDs outrank all classes. Compare left-to-right; the ID tier decides before class count matters.

questions.question: Inline style + !important vs a stylesheet !important: which wins?

options.text: The inline !important wins over a non-inline !important

questions.explanation: Among !important declarations, inline !important beats author !important (a known quirk). Avoid !important to stay sane.

questions.question: To override a third-party rule without !important, you can:

options.text: Increase specificity (add a class/element or use a more specific selector)

questions.explanation: Raising specificity beats the other rule cleanly. BEM-style double-class selectors (.comp .comp-part) are a common tactic.

questions.question: Why is '!important' considered a code smell?

options.text: It breaks the normal cascade, is hard to override, and signals specificity problems

questions.explanation: Overusing !important hides root causes (poor specificity) and creates escalating overrides. Reserve for rare edge cases.

questions.question: The universal selector * and pseudo-class :where() both contribute:
questions.explanation: * and :where() add no specificity, making them safe for resets and easy overrides (unlike :is which adopts inner specificity).

questions.question: Specificity is calculated PER DECLARATION'S SELECTOR, meaning:

options.text: Each selector's specificity is compared independently, not summed across a rule
All selectors on an element are summed

questions.explanation: The winning value comes from the most specific selector that sets that property — selectors for other properties don't add in.

questions.question: Responsive typography means font sizes:

options.text: Scale appropriately across device sizes (not fixed px everywhere)

questions.explanation: Type should adapt to viewport for readability — via media queries, clamp(), or fluid techniques.

questions.question: clamp(1rem, 0.5rem + 1vw, 1.5rem) gives a font size that:

options.text: Is never below 1rem nor above 1.5rem, fluid in between

questions.explanation: clamp(min, preferred, max): the preferred (viewport-based) value is used, bounded by min and max — fluid type without media queries.

questions.question: rem is relative to:
questions.explanation: rem = root em (html font-size). em = parent's font-size. Using rem keeps scaling predictable from the root.

questions.question: em can be tricky because it is relative to:

options.text: The font-size of the element's parent (compounding in nested contexts)

questions.explanation: em references the parent font-size; nested em values compound, which is why rem is often preferred for consistent scaling.

questions.question: Setting html { font-size: 62.5% } is a trick to:

options.text: Make 1rem ≈ 10px so rem math is easier (10px base)

questions.explanation: 62.5% of 16px = 10px, so 1.6rem = 16px. A common convenience (though some prefer leaving 16px base).

questions.question: A modular scale helps by:

options.text: Defining harmonious font-size ratios (e.g. 1.25) across heading levels

questions.explanation: A ratio-based scale produces consistent, pleasing type hierarchy rather than arbitrary sizes.

questions.question: Line-length (measure) best practice is roughly:

options.text: 45-75 characters per line for comfortable reading

questions.explanation: Optimal measure ~45-75 chars; too wide or narrow harms readability. Constrain paragraph max-width accordingly.

questions.question: Viewport-relative units for type include:
questions.explanation: vw scales with viewport width; often combined with clamp()/calc() to avoid extremes on very small/large screens.

questions.question: The three steps of the rendering pipeline are:
questions.explanation: Changing a property can trigger layout (reflow), paint, and/or composite. Fewer stages = better performance.

questions.question: Animating transform/opacity is cheap because they:

options.text: Only trigger compositing (GPU), skipping layout and paint

questions.explanation: transform/opacity are compositor-only properties — the browser promotes the layer and animates on the GPU without reflow/paint.

questions.question: Animating 'width' or 'top' is expensive because it:

options.text: Triggers layout (reflow) which can affect the whole document

questions.explanation: Geometry changes force layout recalculation and often repaint — costly, especially with many elements. Prefer transform.

questions.question: Containment (contain: layout paint) helps by:

options.text: Isolating a subtree so its changes don't reflow/paint the whole page

questions.explanation: contain hints the browser to limit the scope of layout/paint work, improving performance for complex/animated components.

questions.question: will-change should be used:

options.text: Sparingly, only before an expected change, and removed after

questions.explanation: will-change reserves memory/layers; overuse bloats memory and can hurt. Apply just-in-time, not globally.

questions.question: The '60fps' target exists because:

options.text: Most displays refresh ~60 times/sec; hitting it avoids jank

questions.explanation: Smooth animation needs ~16ms per frame. Dropping frames (jank) feels laggy; keep work off the main thread where possible.

questions.question: A long task on the main thread causes:
questions.explanation: Heavy JS/layout work blocks the main thread, starving animation/input — minimize and break up long tasks.

questions.question: prefers-reduced-motion benefits performance AND:
questions.explanation: Reducing motion is primarily an a11y win, and disabling heavy animation also saves battery/CPU.

questions.question: Use a TRANSITION when you want to:

options.text: Smoothly interpolate a property change between two states
Run a multi-step keyframe loop automatically

questions.explanation: Transitions are for state-to-state tweens (hover, toggle). Animations are for keyframe sequences.

questions.question: Use an ANIMATION when you need:

options.text: Multiple keyframe steps, looping, or auto-running on load

questions.explanation: Animations handle sequences, iteration-count, direction, and auto-start — beyond what a transition offers.

questions.question: A transition requires a:
questions.explanation: Transitions are passive — they fire only when a watched property actually changes value.

questions.question: Which can loop infinitely without JS?
questions.explanation: Only keyframe animations support looping/auto-run; transitions always interpolate a single change.

questions.question: Both animations and transitions can be interrupted/reversed by:

options.text: Changing the property again (e.g. removing :hover) — the browser tweens to the new state

questions.explanation: Both are interruptible; reversing the condition smoothly returns to the prior state if transition/timing is defined.

questions.question: Performance-wise, both are fine when animating:
questions.explanation: Whichever you pick, prefer transform/opacity to avoid layout thrash and jank.

questions.question: A loading spinner is best done with:
questions.explanation: Continuous rotation needs a looping keyframe animation (transform: rotate), not a one-shot transition.

questions.question: A button hover color change is best done with:
questions.explanation: A hover color/opacity shift is exactly what transitions are for — no keyframes needed.

questions.question: The two axes in flexbox are:
questions.explanation: flex-direction sets the main axis; the cross axis is perpendicular. justify-content acts on main, align-items on cross.

questions.question: flex-direction: column makes the main axis:
questions.explanation: row/row-reverse are horizontal; column/column-reverse are vertical main axes.

questions.question: justify-content: space-between distributes items with:

options.text: Equal space BETWEEN items, first at start, last at end
Equal space AROUND each item (including edges)

questions.explanation: space-between pushes first/last to edges, equal gaps between. space-around adds half-gaps at edges; space-evenly equalizes all gaps.

questions.question: align-items: stretch (default) makes items:

options.text: Fill the cross-axis (e.g. equal-height columns) when no explicit cross size is set

questions.explanation: Default align-items:stretch stretches items across the cross axis — that's why flex columns are equal height by default.

questions.question: A flex container's direct children become:

options.text: Flex items (blockified, participating in flex layout)

questions.explanation: Children of display:flex are flex items; their display value is blockified (inline elements behave as blocks).

questions.question: flex-basis: auto means the item's base size is:

options.text: Its width/height (or content size if not set)

questions.explanation: flex-basis:auto uses the element's main-size (width for row) if set, else content size — the usual default before grow/shrink.

questions.question: flex-grow distributes:

options.text: Remaining FREE space among items proportional to their grow factors

questions.explanation: After bases are laid out, positive free space is shared per flex-grow. A grow of 2 gets twice a grow of 1.

questions.question: To center a single item in a flex container you set on the CONTAINER:
questions.explanation: Both axes need centering: justify-content (main) + align-items (cross). This is the canonical flex-centering recipe.

questions.question: Calculate specificity of '#nav .item a':
questions.explanation: #nav = 1 ID (0,1,0,0), .item = 1 class (0,0,1,0), a = 1 element (0,0,0,1). Summed tuple = (0,1,1,1).

questions.question: Higher specificity always beats lower even if the lower rule is:
questions.explanation: Specificity outranks source order: a more specific selector wins regardless of where it appears (unless !important enters).

questions.question: Calculate 'ul li span' vs 'ul .item span':

options.text: ul .item span wins (0,0,1,2) vs ul li span (0,0,0,3)

questions.explanation: ul .item span = 1 class + 2 elements (0,0,1,2) beats ul li span = 3 elements (0,0,0,3) because classes outrank elements.

questions.question: p:hover has specificity (0,0,1,1) because:
questions.explanation: :hover is a pseudo-class (class tier). p:hover = element + pseudo-class = (0,0,1,1).

questions.question: Two rules with (0,2,0,1) and (0,1,3,0): which wins?

options.text: (0,2,0,1) — it has more classes (2 > 1), compared at the class tier first

questions.explanation: Compare tier by tier: class tier 2 vs 1 decides; element counts only matter if classes tie.

questions.question: Inline style contributes to which tuple position?
questions.explanation: Inline styles sit in the highest (a) position of (a,b,c,d), beating IDs, classes, and elements.

questions.question: The mnemonic 'ID=100, Class=10, Element=1' is a simplification of:

options.text: Comparing tiers left-to-right (not real base-10 addition)
Actual base-10 math you can sum

questions.explanation: The 100/10/1 heuristic helps intuition but specificity compares tier-by-tier; 11 elements (0,0,0,11) still lose to 1 class (0,0,1,0).

questions.question: To make a rule win without !important and without an ID, you can:

options.text: Add a class or element to raise its specificity above the competitor

questions.explanation: Increment the class/element tier intentionally (e.g. repeat a class or add an ancestor) to outrank the other rule cleanly.

questions.question: The CSS Box Model consists of, from outside in:
questions.explanation: Margin is outermost, then border, then padding, then the content box at the center.

questions.question: With box-sizing: border-box, an element's width includes:

options.text: Padding and border (not margin) — width is the total render size

questions.explanation: border-box makes width/height include padding+border, so sizing is predictable. The modern reset sets this globally.

questions.question: display: inline-block differs from inline in that it:

options.text: Respects width/height and vertical padding/margins (stays on same line)
Breaks to a new line always

questions.explanation: inline-block keeps inline flow but accepts box dimensions — great for nav items, buttons in a row.

questions.question: The default display of <div> is:
questions.explanation: div is block-level (full width, stacks vertically); span is inline.

questions.question: A 'block formatting context' (BFC) is created by, among others:

options.text: overflow: hidden, display: flow-root, or float

questions.explanation: BFCs isolate layout (contain floats, prevent margin collapse). display:flow-root creates one cleanly without side effects.

questions.question: Margin collapsing means:

options.text: Adjacent vertical margins of block siblings combine into the larger one

questions.explanation: Vertical margins between siblings (and parent-child in some cases) collapse to the max of the two — a classic layout surprise.

questions.question: To center a block horizontally you use:
questions.explanation: margin: 0 auto centers a fixed-width block; text-align:center only centers inline content.

questions.question: float was originally designed for:

options.text: Wrapping text around images (later abused for full layouts)

questions.explanation: float was for text-wrapping; modern layouts use flex/grid. Clearfix or BFC contains floated children.

questions.question: box-sizing: border-box makes width include:
questions.explanation: With border-box, the declared width is the total box size; padding/border are subtracted internally. Margin stays outside.

questions.question: An element with width:100px, padding:10px, border:2px, box-sizing:content-box renders at total width:
questions.explanation: content-box adds padding+border to the width, so 100+20+4 = 124px total.

questions.question: Padding is the space:

options.text: Between the content and the border (inside the box)

questions.explanation: Padding is inner spacing (content→border). Margin is outer (border→neighbors).

questions.question: Margin is the space:

options.text: Outside the border, separating the element from others

questions.explanation: Margin is the outermost spacing; it is transparent and pushes siblings away. Not part of the element's background.

questions.question: A common reset is:

options.text: * { box-sizing: border-box; } so widths are predictable

questions.explanation: The universal border-box reset makes sizing intuitive across the app — a near-universal best practice.

questions.question: Background (color/image) fills:
questions.explanation: Background extends through padding to the border edge; margin is always transparent and outside the background.

questions.question: box-sizing: content-box is the:

options.text: Default (CSS spec) value — width applies to content only

questions.explanation: The initial value is content-box; that's why a reset to border-box is so common.

questions.question: Total element outer width equals:
questions.explanation: Outer footprint = the box (content+padding+border) plus margin on each side. Border-box width already includes the first three.

questions.question: rem is relative to:
questions.explanation: rem = root em. Scaling html font-size resizes all rem-based dimensions consistently.

questions.question: em in font-size is relative to:
questions.explanation: When set on font-size, em references the parent's font-size. (In other properties, em references the element's own font-size.)

questions.question: vw means:
questions.explanation: vw = viewport width unit; 100vw = full width. vh is height. Great for fluid type/layout.

questions.question: A pitfall of 100vw is:

options.text: It includes the vertical scrollbar width, causing horizontal overflow

questions.explanation: 100vw counts the scrollbar, so a 100vw element can be slightly wider than the visible area → horizontal scroll. Use max-width:100% or 100% where possible.

questions.question: % is relative to:
questions.explanation: Percentage widths are relative to the parent's width; heights to parent's height (when defined).

questions.question: vmin / vmax are relative to:

options.text: The smaller / larger of the viewport width and height

questions.explanation: vmin = 1% of the smaller viewport dimension; vmax = 1% of the larger. Useful for square/full-bleed elements.

questions.question: Why prefer rem for spacing/typography in a scalable system?

options.text: A single root size change scales the whole UI predictably (no em compounding)

questions.explanation: rem avoids the compounding problem of nested em, so resizing the root scales everything uniformly.

questions.question: ch unit equals the width of:

options.text: The '0' (zero) glyph of the element's font

questions.explanation: ch is the advance width of '0'; handy for sizing inputs/paragraphs to a character count (e.g. max-width: 60ch).

questions.question: The shorthand 'transition: all 0.3s ease' sets, in order:
questions.explanation: transition shorthand order is property duration timing-function delay (duration is required; others optional).

questions.question: Which is REQUIRED for a transition to occur?
questions.explanation: Without duration > 0 the change is instant. Timing-function and delay are optional with defaults.

questions.question: transition-delay: 0.5s means the transition:

options.text: Starts half a second AFTER the property change

questions.explanation: delay postpones the start; duration sets length. They are separate components of the shorthand.

questions.question: transition-timing-function: ease is a:

options.text: Preset curve that starts slow, speeds up, ends slow

questions.explanation: ease is the default; linear is constant; ease-in/out/inception curves vary. cubic-bezier gives full control.

questions.question: To animate on page load you should use:

options.text: An animation, not a transition (transitions need a trigger/change)

questions.explanation: Transitions only run on a value change; for entrance animations on load, keyframe animations (or toggling a class via JS) are needed.

questions.question: transition: none disables:

options.text: All transitions so changes are instant

questions.explanation: transition: none removes the transition entirely — useful to disable motion (e.g. under reduced-motion).

questions.question: Transitioning 'height: auto' is problematic because:

options.text: auto is not animatable; you need a fixed height or max-height technique

questions.explanation: auto has no intermediate value to interpolate. Animate max-height (to a safe upper bound) or use grid 0fr→1fr / JS for collapsing.

questions.question: Combining transitions with :focus-visible improves:

options.text: Keyboard accessibility (smooth cues only for keyboard users)

questions.explanation: :focus-visible shows focus rings for keyboard nav (not mouse), so transitioned focus styles aid a11y without noise for mouse users.

questions.question: @media (max-width: 600px) applies when the viewport is:
questions.explanation: max-width is inclusive of the value: styles apply at 600px and below (mobile-first uses min-width instead).

questions.question: Mobile-first CSS typically uses:

options.text: min-width queries (base styles for small, enhance upward)

questions.explanation: Mobile-first: write base for small screens, then min-width breakpoints add layouts for larger devices.

questions.question: The 'only screen' prefix is used to:

options.text: Hide the query from very old browsers that don't support media queries

questions.explanation: only prevents legacy browsers from applying the styles; mostly historical now but still harmless.

questions.question: Media features can be combined with:
questions.explanation: Use 'and' to require multiple features, commas for OR (independent queries), and 'not' to negate.

questions.question: prefers-color-scheme: dark targets users who:

options.text: Have their OS set to dark mode

questions.explanation: prefers-color-scheme (dark/light) reads the OS theme — pairs with CSS variables for automatic dark mode.

questions.question: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce signals the user wants:
questions.explanation: Respect it by disabling/reducing non-essential motion — critical for users sensitive to movement.

questions.question: An orientation: portrait query matches when:

options.text: The viewport height is greater than or equal to its width

questions.explanation: portrait = taller than wide; landscape = wider than tall. Commonly used for layout swaps on phones.

questions.question: Breakpoints should ideally be based on:

options.text: Your content/layout needs, not specific device widths

questions.explanation: Design for content breakpoints (where the layout breaks), not a fixed list of devices — more future-proof.

questions.question: position: relative offsets an element:

options.text: From its NORMAL position, leaving its original space occupied

questions.explanation: relative shifts visually via top/left/right/bottom but keeps its spot in flow (also establishes a positioning context for absolutes).

questions.question: position: absolute takes an element:

options.text: Out of normal flow, positioned relative to nearest positioned ancestor

questions.explanation: absolute removes the element from flow; it anchors to the nearest ancestor with position != static, else the initial containing block.

questions.question: position: fixed anchors to:

options.text: The viewport (stays put on scroll), unless an ancestor has a transform

questions.explanation: fixed positions relative to the viewport; an ancestor with transform/filter creates a containing block, breaking the viewport anchor.

questions.question: position: sticky behaves like:

options.text: relative until it crosses a threshold, then sticks like fixed within its parent

questions.explanation: sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll position, constrained to its containing parent — great for headers.

questions.question: z-index only affects elements with:

options.text: A positioning value other than static (or flex/grid items)

questions.explanation: z-index applies to positioned elements (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky) and flex/grid items; static elements ignore it.

questions.question: z-index stacking context is created by, among others:

options.text: position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, will-change, filter

questions.explanation: Many properties create a new stacking context, trapping child z-index within it — a common 'why won't it overlap' gotcha.

questions.question: To center with absolute positioning you can use:
questions.explanation: The translate(-50%,-50%) trick offsets by the element's own size to truly center it within the positioned ancestor.

questions.question: A common use of position: relative is:

options.text: Creating a positioning context for absolutely-positioned children (tooltips, badges)

questions.explanation: Setting a wrapper to relative lets child absolutes anchor to it instead of the viewport — essential for overlays/badges.

questions.question: transform: translate(10px, 20px) moves an element:
questions.explanation: translate(x, y): positive x is right, positive y is down. Transforms are visual only — they don't affect surrounding layout.

questions.question: transform-origin controls:

options.text: The point around which rotate/scale/skew operations happen

questions.explanation: Default origin is center; changing it (e.g. top left) changes how rotation/scaling pivots.

questions.question: transform: scale(1.5) makes the element:

options.text: 1.5× its size (visual only, layout space unchanged)

questions.explanation: scale multiplies dimensions visually; surrounding layout is unaffected (unlike width/height which reflows).

questions.question: Multiple transforms on one element are applied:

options.text: Right-to-left as a combined matrix (e.g. translate then rotate order matters)

questions.explanation: transform: translate() rotate() applies right-to-left; order changes the result (rotate-then-translate differs from translate-then-rotate).

questions.question: transform: rotate(45deg) rotates:
questions.explanation: Positive angles rotate clockwise (in standard screen coords). Negative rotates counter-clockwise.

questions.question: A transform creates a new:

options.text: Stacking context and containing block (affects fixed descendants)

questions.explanation: Applying transform establishes a stacking context and a containing block — so position:fixed children anchor to it, not the viewport.

questions.question: To flip horizontally you use:
questions.explanation: scaleX(-1) mirrors along the X axis. rotate(180) flips both axes; for horizontal-only use scaleX(-1).

questions.question: Transforms are GPU-friendly because they:

options.text: Run on the compositor layer (no layout/paint per frame)

questions.explanation: translate/rotate/scale/opacity animate on the compositor — that's why they're the preferred animation properties for smoothness.

questions.question: A linear-gradient(90deg, red, blue) goes from:

options.text: Red on the LEFT to blue on the RIGHT (0deg = top→bottom, 90deg = left→right)
Red on top to blue bottom only

questions.explanation: Angle 0deg points up (bottom→top); 90deg points right (left→right). 90deg = red left, blue right.

questions.question: background-size: cover means the image:

options.text: Scales to fill the area, cropping overflow to preserve aspect ratio
Fits entirely inside, possibly leaving gaps

questions.explanation: cover fills the box (cropping edges); contain fits the whole image (may letterbox). repeat tiles.

questions.question: Multiple backgrounds are layered with:
questions.explanation: background: url(a), linear-gradient(...) stacks them; the first listed is painted front-most.

questions.question: background-clip: text makes the background visible:

options.text: Only within the glyphs (text shows the gradient) when combined with transparent text color

questions.explanation: clipping to text + color: transparent lets a gradient fill the letters — a popular text-effect technique.

questions.question: radial-gradient creates a:

options.text: Circular/elliptical gradient radiating from a center point

questions.explanation: radial-gradient spreads from a center outward (circle or ellipse), useful for glows, spotlights, buttons.

questions.question: repeating-linear-gradient is useful for:

options.text: Stripes/patterns that tile the gradient automatically

questions.explanation: repeating-* gradients loop the color stops, ideal for zebra stripes, rulers, and patterns without images.

questions.question: background-position: center center places the image:
questions.explanation: Two-value position sets x and y; 'center center' centers the image in the box (with no-repeat).

questions.question: Gradients are technically:

options.text: CSS images (so they work anywhere an image is accepted)

questions.explanation: Gradients are <image> values — usable in background, border-image, mask, etc. They're not separate files.
